title: Learn AI from scratch: concepts and key skills
tagline: AI concepts, skills and a starter plan for beginners
lede: Everything a beginner needs to understand AI and use it well: the core ideas in plain English, the skills worth building, and a realistic plan to get there.
description: Learn AI from scratch: LLMs, tokens, context windows and RAG in plain English, the skills that matter, how long it takes, and how to tell when AI is wrong.
intro: Learning AI sounds like a technical project. For most people it isn't. You don't need to build models. You need to understand roughly how tools like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini work, what they're good and bad at, and how to direct and check them.

This hub is the beginner's map. The guide below explains the core concepts in plain English, the skills that matter, how long it really takes and a plan to start this week. Every post in the hub goes deeper on one piece, so read in order or jump to your gap.

guide.heading: What learning AI actually means
guide.html:
There are two very different things people mean by learning AI, and picking the right one saves you months.

  • Using AI. Prompting, choosing the right tool, judging the output and applying it to real work. No code needed, and it pays off within weeks.
  • Building AI. Training and fine-tuning models. That path needs programming (usually Python), maths and machine learning, and takes months to years.

Almost everyone means the first one. If that's you, start with how to learn AI without coding, and if you're still deciding whether it's worth your time at all, read is learning AI worth it.

Two words come up constantly. AI literacy is understanding what AI is, what it can and can't do and how to use it responsibly. AI fluency is being able to use it well in practice. Literacy is knowing a model can make things up. Fluency is getting a good answer and catching the one fact it got wrong. You want both, and this hub covers both.

guide.heading: The core concepts in plain English
guide.html:
You don't need the maths. You do need a working mental model, because it explains most of the strange things AI does. These are the terms worth knowing first.

TermWhat it meansWhy it matters to you
AI, machine learning, deep learningNested ideas: deep learning is a type of machine learning, which is the main way we build AI todayToday's tools learn from data, so they reflect its gaps and can be confidently wrong
Generative AIAI that creates new text, images, audio, video or code from a promptIt produces plausible output, not verified facts
LLMA large language model, trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next wordIt's the engine inside ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Perplexity
TokenA chunk of text, often a word or part of onePricing, limits and context windows are all counted in tokens
Context windowHow much text a model can consider at onceLong chats drift because the oldest parts fall out of view
RAGRetrieval-augmented generation: the AI looks up real sources before answeringCited, grounded answers are easier to check and generally more trustworthy

Each has its own short explainer. Start with AI vs machine learning vs deep learning and what generative AI is, then what an LLM is. A useful rule of thumb from what tokens are: in English, about 1,000 tokens covers roughly 750 words. What a context window is explains why a chat seems to forget your early instructions, and what RAG is explains why tools that show sources behave differently from ones that don't.

For anything else, the AI glossary has plain-language definitions, and how to learn LLMs goes one level deeper on the models themselves.

guide.heading: The skills that matter more than the theory
guide.html:
Concepts help you understand AI. Skills change what you get out of it. The seven that matter most, from the AI skills worth learning in 2026, are all communication and judgment, not code:

  1. Prompting: turning a vague need into clear instructions.
  2. Tool choice: knowing which assistant fits which job.
  3. Output judgment: telling a good answer from a confident wrong one.
  4. Verification: checking facts, numbers and sources before relying on them.
  5. Workflow design: folding AI into how you already work.
  6. Working with AI agents: knowing when to hand over a multi-step task, and where agents fail.
  7. Continuous learning: picking up whatever comes next, quickly.

The AI Fluency Pyramid shows how these stack, in five levels: Access, Operation, Direction, Judgment and Leverage. Most people stall at Operation, typing a question and taking whatever comes back, and decide AI is overhyped. The biggest jump is from Operation to Direction, which is mostly one habit: stop asking, start directing.

Prompting is the highest-leverage of the seven, so it has its own hub: prompt engineering patterns, examples and practice. For a step-by-step route to fluency, see how to become AI fluent.

guide.heading: How long it takes to learn AI
guide.html:
Faster than most people expect, if you mean using AI rather than building it. With about five focused minutes a day on real tasks, a realistic timeline from how long it takes to learn AI looks like this:

  • Week 1: get comfortable. One tool, real tasks, a basic prompt structure.
  • Weeks 2 to 3: get useful. Sharper prompts, catching obvious mistakes, saving real time.
  • Month 2: get broad. A second and third tool, and your own use cases.
  • Month 3 and beyond: get fluent. AI is a default part of how you work, and you know when to trust it.

Specialising in an area like marketing, finance or agents adds a few weeks on top. Building models is a different timeline entirely.

The variable that matters most is consistency. Short daily practice compounds faster than an occasional weekend binge, which is the whole idea behind learning AI in 5 minutes a day.

guide.heading: A 30-day plan to get started
guide.html:
If you want a concrete starting point, the 30-day beginner plan builds judgment one week at a time. You only need a free account on one assistant.

  1. Week 1, get comfortable. Use one assistant for one small real task a day: an email, a summary, a plan. Reps, not perfection.
  2. Week 2, prompt with structure. Tell the model who to be, what you want and what the output must do or avoid. Rewrite last week's vague prompts and compare.
  3. Week 3, verify everything. Each day, take one factual claim an AI gave you and check it before you trust it.
  4. Week 4, build a workflow. Pick a recurring task and design a simple draft, critique, finalise loop you'll actually reuse.

The method matters as much as the plan. Write prompts yourself instead of watching someone else do it, use real tasks so the lessons stick, and get feedback quickly. Iro is built around exactly that loop: short, gamified lessons on iPhone and the web, with feedback on every exercise. The longer version of this roadmap is how to learn AI in 2026.

guide.heading: How to tell when AI is wrong
guide.html:
An AI hallucination is a confident, plausible answer that's false. It isn't a glitch you can switch off: LLMs generate the most likely text, not verified facts, so a made-up answer looks exactly as confident as a true one. Your job is to supply the doubt the model doesn't.

The quick checks from how to spot AI hallucinations in 5 seconds:

  • Treat any name, date, statistic, quote or citation as a hypothesis until you've checked it.
  • Be suspicious of confident claims about recent events, niche topics or private information the model couldn't know.
  • Click through citations. Fake ones look real on the surface.
  • Cross-check important facts with a search-grounded tool that shows sources.
  • Push back with the opposite claim. If the model flips straight away, the first answer wasn't grounded.

For anything you're sending, signing or quoting, do the deeper checks too. This is the Judgment level of the pyramid, and it's what makes AI safe to rely on.

guide.heading: Spotting AI-generated content
guide.html:
The flip side of using AI is recognising it. There's no fully reliable way to detect AI content, and detection tools both miss it and flag genuine human writing. Treat a detector score as a weak signal, never a verdict.

Common tells, covered in how to tell if something is AI-generated:

  • Text: generic, hedge-heavy phrasing, confident factual slips, repetition, and smooth structure that says very little.
  • Images: odd hands and teeth, garbled lettering, lighting that doesn't match, and backgrounds that melt together.

These tells fade as models improve. The habit that lasts is to stop asking whether a machine wrote something and start asking whether it's true. Check the specific claims against reputable sources, whoever wrote them.

guide.heading: Are AI certificates worth it?
guide.html:
Usually not, unless someone else is paying or a job posting asks for one. That's the honest summary of are AI certifications worth it, and it's worth knowing that most articles on the question come from people selling certificates.

A certificate gives you a syllabus, a line on your profile and a keyword for screening software. It doesn't prove you can use AI well. People hiring for AI skills tend to ask three things instead: what have you built with it, can you tell when it's wrong, and how well do you know the tools your team actually uses.

So if you have a training budget, use it. If a specific role names a credential, get the cheapest one that fits. Otherwise, put the time into building something real and writing up the decisions you made.

guide.heading: How to keep up without chasing every release
guide.html:
The tools change monthly. The direction is steadier: the big AI trends in 2026 are agents that take multi-step actions, models that handle text, images and voice together, AI built into everyday apps, and stronger reasoning. Each one raises the value of directing and checking AI well, not lowering it.

You don't need to try every new model. Keep a small daily practice habit, learn new tools as you need them, and apply what you learn to real work. AI for work covers the job-specific side.

To find your starting point, take the free AI literacy test. It takes about two minutes and shows your weakest topic. Curious how other people do? We publish the results in our AI literacy score report. Then pick one gap and close it, a few minutes a day. That's what Iro is for.

faq.q: Can I learn AI without coding?
faq.a: Yes. Using AI tools well is a language-and-judgment skill: prompting, choosing the right tool and checking the output. Coding only matters if you want to build or fine-tune models yourself.

faq.q: How long does it take to learn AI?
faq.a: With about five focused minutes a day, most people become genuinely useful with AI tools in two to three weeks and feel confident within a few months. Learning to build AI models is a separate path that takes months to years.
Pick one assistant and use it on a real task every day, then learn a simple prompt structure: context, role, task and format. Add verification habits early so you know when not to trust an answer.

faq.q: What is the difference between AI and machine learning?
faq.a: AI is the broad goal of machines doing tasks that seem intelligent. Machine learning is the main way we build it, by learning patterns from data, and deep learning is a type of machine learning that powers most of today's generative AI.

faq.q: What is the difference between AI literacy and AI fluency?
faq.a: AI literacy is understanding what AI is, what it can and can't do and how to use it responsibly. AI fluency is being able to use it well in practice. Literacy keeps you safe; fluency makes you effective.

faq.q: How do I know if an AI answer is wrong?
faq.a: Treat names, dates, numbers, quotes and citations as unverified until you check them. Cross-check important claims with a tool that cites sources, and be wary of confident answers about recent events or niche topics.
Usually only if your employer pays or a job posting asks for one. Something you built with AI and can explain tends to carry more weight than a certificate.

faq.q: Can AI detectors tell if something was written by AI?
faq.a: Not reliably. They miss AI text and wrongly flag human writing, so treat any score as a weak signal and focus on checking whether the content is accurate.
